text: Some time later Absalom acquired a chariot and horses, along with fifty men to run ahead of him.

He would rise early and stand beside the road leading to the city gate. Whenever anyone came with a case to bring before the king for judgment, Absalom would call out to him and ask, "What town are you from?" And when the man answered, "Your servant is from one of the tribes of Israel,"

versions.text: He would rise early and stand beside the road leading to the city gate. Whenever anyone came with a case to bring before the king for judgment, Absalom would call out to him and ask, "What town are you from?" And when the man answered, "Your servant is from such and such a tribe of Israel,"
versions.explanation: The Hebrew says "from one of the tribes of Israel." "Such and such" is a vaguer paraphrase and reads less naturally aloud; the literal wording is both clearer and smoother.

text: Absalom would say to him, "Look, your claims are good and right, but the king has appointed no one to hear you."
And Absalom would add, "If only I were made judge in this land! Then everyone with a case or a claim could come to me, and I would see that he got justice."
And whenever a man approached to bow down before him, Absalom would reach out his hand, take hold of him, and kiss him.
This is how Absalom treated every Israelite who came to the king for judgment, and so he stole the hearts of the people of Israel.
At the end of four years Absalom said to the king, "Let me go to Hebron and fulfill the vow I made to the LORD.
For while your servant was living in Geshur in Aram, I made this vow: 'If the LORD brings me back to Jerusalem, I will worship the LORD.'"
The king said to him, "Go in peace." So he set out for Hebron.
Then Absalom sent messengers secretly throughout all the tribes of Israel with this word: "As soon as you hear the sound of the ram's horn, say, 'Absalom is king in Hebron!'"
Two hundred men from Jerusalem went with Absalom. They had been invited as guests and went in all innocence, knowing nothing of the matter.

Absalom also sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's counselor, to come from his town of Giloh. And while Absalom was offering the sacrifices, the conspiracy gained strength, and his following kept growing.
A messenger came to David and reported, "The hearts of the men of Israel have gone over to Absalom."

Then David said to all his officials who were with him in Jerusalem, "Come, we must flee, or none of us will escape from Absalom. Go quickly, or he will overtake us, bring disaster down on us, and put the city to the sword."
The king's servants answered him, "Whatever our lord the king decides, your servants are ready."
So the king set out on foot, and his whole household with him, but he left behind ten concubines to look after the palace.
The king went out on foot with all the people following him, and they stopped at the last house.
All his servants passed by him, along with all the Kerethites and Pelethites, and all six hundred Gittites who had come with him from Gath marched past the king.
The king said to Ittai the Gittite, "Why should you come along with us? Go back and stay with the king. You are a foreigner, an exile from your own land.
You came only yesterday. Should I make you wander with us today, when I am going wherever I can? Go back, and take your countrymen with you, and may steadfast love and faithfulness go with you.

versions.text: You came only yesterday. Should I make you wander with us today, when I myself do not know where I am going? Go back, and take your countrymen with you. May the LORD show you steadfast love and faithfulness."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew reads "I am going wherever I go," not that David does not know his destination, and the closing phrase is simply "steadfast love and faithfulness" (the words "May the LORD show you" come from ancient versions). If the current interpretive rendering is kept, a footnote noting the Hebrew wording would help.

text: But Ittai answered the king, "As surely as the LORD lives, and as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king may be, whether it means life or death, there your servant will be."
David said to Ittai, "Very well, march on." So Ittai the Gittite marched on with all his men and all the children who were with him.
The whole countryside wept aloud as all the people passed by. The king crossed the Kidron Valley, and all the people moved on toward the wilderness.

Zadok was also there, and with him all the Levites, carrying the ark of the covenant of God. They set down the ark of God, and Abiathar offered sacrifices until all the people had finished leaving the city.
Then the king said to Zadok, "Take the ark of God back into the city. If I find favor in the LORD's eyes, he will bring me back and let me see both it and his dwelling place again.
But if he says, 'I am not pleased with you,' then here I am; let him do to me whatever seems good to him."
The king also said to Zadok the priest, "Listen: go back to the city in peace, and take with you your son Ahimaaz and Jonathan son of Abiathar—your two sons.
I will wait at the fords in the wilderness until word comes from you to inform me."
So Zadok and Abiathar took the ark of God back to Jerusalem and stayed there.
But David went on up the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went, his head covered and his feet bare. And all the people with him covered their heads and went up, weeping as they went.
When David was told that Ahithophel was among the conspirators with Absalom, he prayed, "LORD, turn Ahithophel's counsel into folly."
When David reached the summit, where people used to worship God, Hushai the Arkite was there to meet him, his robe torn and dust on his head.
David said to him, "If you go with me, you will only be a burden to me.

But if you return to the city and say to Absalom, 'I will be your servant, O king; as I was your father's servant in the past, so now I will be your servant,' then you can frustrate Ahithophel's counsel for me.

versions.text: But if you return to the city and say to Absalom, 'I am your servant, my king; I was your father's servant before, but now I am yours,' then you can frustrate Ahithophel's counsel for me.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew includes the verb אֶהְיֶה ('I will be'), a pledge of future loyalty, which is dropped in 'I am your servant.' Also הַמֶּלֶךְ is a vocative address ('O king') rather than the possessive 'my king,' and the second clause repeats 'your servant' for emphasis.

text: Won't the priests Zadok and Abiathar be there with you? Report to them everything you hear in the king's palace.
Their two sons are with them, Ahimaaz son of Zadok and Jonathan son of Abiathar. Through them send word to me of everything you hear."

versions.text: Their two sons are with them, Ahimaaz son of Zadok and Jonathan son of Abiathar. Send them to me with everything you hear."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew says to send the message 'by their hand' — the sons are the couriers, not the thing sent. 'Send them to me' reads as if the sons themselves are the object of the sending, which blurs the sense. Note also that the speech ends with a closing quotation mark here, but no opening quotation mark appears at the start of the quoted speech in verses 34-35, which is inconsistent for oral reading.

text: So Hushai, David's friend, arrived in the city just as Absalom was entering Jerusalem.
